questions.question: In a Jordan block $J(λ)$, where do the λ entries appear?
Where are the 1s placed in a standard Jordan block?
Why is every Jordan block upper triangular?
options: Its only nonzero entries lie on the main diagonal.
All entries below the main diagonal are zero.
It is symmetric, so both triangles match.
All entries above the diagonal are zero.

questions.question: What do Jordan blocks build inside Jordan normal form?
options: They are coefficient matrices of linear systems only.
They are the diagonal building pieces of Jordan normal form.
They are the off-diagonal blocks that couple different eigenvalues.
They are row-operation matrices used for elimination.

questions.question: What does the size of a Jordan block reflect?
options: The number of different eigenvalues of the whole matrix
The algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda$ as a root of the characteristic polynomial
The number of independent ordinary eigenvectors for $\lambda$
The length of its Jordan chain of generalized eigenvectors

questions.question: Which matrix is a $2\times2$ Jordan block with eigenvalue 4?
What is the eigenvalue of $\begin{pmatrix}7&1\\0&7\end{pmatrix}$ as a Jordan block?
In the $3\times3$ Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}λ&1&0\\0&λ&1\\0&0&λ\end{pmatrix}$, how many superdiagonal 1s are there?
Which entry must be zero in a $3\times3$ Jordan block?
What is the determinant of the $2\times2$ Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}λ&1\\0&λ\end{pmatrix}$?
Does a Jordan block of size greater than 1 have enough independent ordinary eigenvectors to be diagonal by itself?
options: Yes. Every Jordan block is already diagonal
Yes, because all diagonal entries are equal
No, because a repeated eigenvalue always rules out a diagonal form
No. The superdiagonal 1s signal generalized eigenvectors

questions.question: How is a $1\times1$ Jordan block different from a larger block?
options: It is $(1)$ for every eigenvalue, like an identity block.
It cannot appear in a Jordan normal form.
It is just $(λ)$ and has no superdiagonal 1s.
It is $(\lambda)$ with a single superdiagonal $1$.

questions.question: Why can the eigenvalues of a Jordan block be read from its diagonal?
options: It is symmetric, and symmetric matrices have diagonal eigenvalues.
It is upper triangular, so the diagonal holds its eigenvalues.
Its trace equals the eigenvalue sum, so each diagonal entry is an eigenvalue.
Its $1$s above the diagonal are eigenvalues as well, next to $\lambda$.

questions.question: What is the characteristic polynomial of $\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$?
For a $4\times4$ Jordan block $J(2)$, how many entries equal 1 immediately above the diagonal?
Which matrix is not a Jordan block?
What part of a Jordan block prevents it from being diagonal when the block has size at least 2?
options: The repeated $\lambda$ along the main diagonal.
The nonzero value of $\lambda$ on the diagonal.
The zeros below the main diagonal.

questions.question: How does a Jordan block encode a chain rather than just a single eigenvector?
options: Its diagonal holds a different eigenvalue for each chain vector
Its columns are the chain vectors, all ordinary eigenvectors
Its zeros below the diagonal record the steps of the chain

questions.question: Let $J=\begin{pmatrix}λ&1&0\\0&λ&1\\0&0&λ\end{pmatrix}$. What is $J-λI$?
For $J=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is $(J-2I)^2$?
